votes.lens: right-sized (over- vs under-engineering for the real data scale and a solo TS/Node builder who hates over-engineering)
votes.reasoning:
The DECISION is right-sized and the codebase already landed on it: the tower design (tower/research/2026-06-27-03-tower-design.md:44,153,181) specifies a SQLite RunRecord store, with RunRecord defined as "one immutable row per agent_version x tower_version x N_rep batch" (tower/research/raw/strand3-design-B.md:238), append-only and CI-carrying, behind a storage-agnostic ResultSink.put(record) interface with an explicit named graduation trigger "SQLite -> Postgres -> object store." That is textbook right-sizing: matches real scale + names the escape hatch.

Three load-bearing facts make SQLite correct and DuckDB over-engineering here:
1) Scale. DuckDB's columnar/vectorized advantage only activates at millions of rows / wide BI scans (primary sources). At tens-to-thousands of rows ANY engine scans the whole table in microseconds, so the analytical engine's one benefit never fires while its costs (heavier native dep, unfamiliar SQL dialect for a TS/Node builder, weaker single-row insert path) are paid up front. better-sqlite3 is the builder's daily-driver embedded store. Bringing DuckDB = importing an OLAP platform for a dataset that fits in a spreadsheet -> over-engineering, correctly rejected.
2) Write pattern. RunRecords are emitted one immutable row per batch — single-row appends. Primary sources confirm DuckDB is architecturally a mismatch for high-frequency single-row inserts (it is batch/bulk-load oriented); SQLite's row-oriented transactional insert is the mechanically apt path. So SQLite wins on the write side independent of read scale.
3) Durability/CI. The append-only immutable design + SQLite's ACID single-file store does NOT under-provision: data is durable, no loss, git can track the file. The graduation path correctly points to Postgres/object-store (concurrency/durability/multi-writer concerns) rather than DuckDB — consistent, because any future bottleneck is write-concurrency, not analytical scan speed.

ONE HONEST CORRECTION to the claim's reasoning (does not flip the verdict): the QUERY itself (GROUP BY tool+level over time, CI comparison) is actually analytically/aggregation-SHAPED — GROUP BY is the canonical OLAP operation — so calling it "OLTP-shaped, not OLAP-shaped" is the imprecise label for the right answer. SQLite wins here not because the workload is transactional, but because (a) the dataset is orders of magnitude below DuckDB's columnar break-even and (b) the write pattern is single-row append (DuckDB's weak spot). Same conclusion, sturdier reason. Under the right-sized lens — matches real scale, fits the builder's stack, durable, with a named graduation trigger, and correctly refuses an OLAP engine whose strengths this data never exercises — the claim holds: confirmed.

votes.claim: The RunRecord query pattern is OLTP-shaped at this scale (tens-to-low-thousands of rows), so a row-oriented SQLite store is the correct fit and DuckDB's columnar vectorized engine solves the wrong problem.
votes.lens: durability — survives without loss/drift/irreproducibility; backed up; artifacts on the filesystem by path (not DB blobs); the human-facing index can't silently drift from the store
votes.reasoning:
Through the durability lens the decision survives, with one addressable residual.

WHY IT SURVIVES. SQLite is one of the most durable storage technologies in existence: a Library-of-Congress Recommended Storage Format, full ACID (atomic, crash-durable via WAL), bit-for-bit identical files across 32/64-bit and endianness, public-domain, with a developer pledge to support the format through 2050 (sqlite.org/locrsf.html, /aff_short.html, /lts.html). DuckDB only reached a backward-compat *storage-format stability guarantee* at v1.0 in June 2024, with forward-compat still "best effort" (duckdb.org/docs/.../storage, /2024/06/03/announcing-duckdb-100). So on pure survival, SQLite is the stronger bet AND DuckDB is the weaker one — rejecting DuckDB is additionally justified on durability grounds beyond the OLTP/OLAP argument. For tens-to-thousands of append-only rows you would be paying DuckDB's later-stabilized columnar format and analytics-engine surface for vectorized scan power the scale never exercises: the "wrong problem" framing holds.

WHY DURABILITY IS CONCRETELY HANDLED. The claim itself is narrow (query-shape only) and silent on backups/reproducibility/artifacts — but the surrounding spec is not. The RunRecord is append-only and CI-carrying, and every row pins agentVersion/towerVersion/taskSetHash/graderVersions/envFingerprint/ipClass/handoffMode (tower/research/2026-06-27-03-tower-design.md:139), which is reproducibility baked into the schema. The Strand-4 mandate explicitly requires "backups for results; artifacts on filesystem referenced by path — never blobs in the DB" (docs/specs/2026-06-27-bench-reframe-and-research-loop-design.md:84). Neither requirement is harmed by the SQLite choice; both are equally satisfiable in SQLite. No loss or irreproducibility risk is introduced.

THE ONE RESIDUAL (not a refutation, but fix it). SQLite is a *binary* file, while the spec's own discipline is "git for text/artifacts" and the committed scoreboard tower/results.md is markdown. A binary store does not git-diff, so provenance review is opaque and the human-facing index CAN silently drift from the store unless results.md is a deterministic projection regenerated from RunRecord (plus a CI/check that fails on drift). At this exact scale the spec's own survey nominates the cleaner durability option the claim omits via a false SQLite-vs-DuckDB binary: append-only JSONL/NDJSON — itself a LoC-recommended (JSON) family — is human-readable, git-diffable, corruption-resilient on append, and trivially backed up. Recommendation: keep SQLite as the query/index layer if you want SQL convenience, but treat an append-only JSONL RunRecord log as the source of truth committed to git, make results.md a regenerated projection, and keep run artifacts (screenshots/PNGs) on the filesystem by path as already mandated. That closes the drift gap. None of this rises to loss/irreproducibility, so the verdict is confirmed, not refuted.

votes.lens: prior-art (is there a standard maintained tool/pattern to reuse, or is this reinventing/cargo-culting?)
votes.reasoning:
The DECISION is sound by the prior-art lens: SQLite is the canonical, maintained, right-sized standard for a small embedded append-only structured store, and choosing it over DuckDB is NOT cargo-culting a heavy tool (DuckDB is the heavier/columnar option being correctly declined) and NOT reinventing anything. DuckDB's own docs position it as OLAP-only, single-writer, and explicitly recommend SQLite/Postgres for transactional/point workloads (https://duckdb.org/docs/current/connect/concurrency), so SQLite is the appropriate standard here.

However the REASONING that justifies it is partly wrong and should not be accepted as stated: (1) The query is MISLABELED. `GROUP BY tool+level+score OVER TIME` with aggregation is the textbook OLAP/analytical read shape, not OLTP — the only OLTP-ish part is the trivial append of one immutable RunRecord per batch. So the read side actually leans toward DuckDB's strength, not away from it. (2) 'DuckDB solves the wrong problem' is overstated: what makes DuckDB unnecessary is SCALE, not query shape — at thousands of rows the columnar/vectorized advantage is unmeasurable (both engines return sub-millisecond), and DuckDB's single-writer batch-append model would fit this write pattern fine too. DuckDB is unnecessary, not wrong.

Net: right tool, muddled rationale. The honest framing is 'at this scale the engine's performance profile is irrelevant; pick the simplest durable standard.' That correctly selects SQLite — but it equally surfaces a lighter prior-art the claim ignores: at tens-to-low-thousands of immutable JSON records, the most minimal standard is NO SQL engine at all (JSONL/NDJSON or Parquet read into memory, aggregated in TS), which the design already half-commits to ('git for text/artifacts', 'artifacts on filesystem by path'). SQLite is still defensible and not over-engineering (single-file, ACID, free SQL for the group-by), and the storage-agnostic ResultSink.put(record) seam makes the choice cheap to revisit. Verdict confirmed on the tool selection, with the caveat that the OLTP-vs-OLAP framing is the wrong axis — scale is.

votes.claim: Clopper-Pearson CI math belongs in TypeScript as pure functions (ci_lo, ci_hi stored as REAL columns), not in SQL — so the DB engine has zero bearing on statistical correctness and the leaderboard fold is a straightforward SQL GROUP BY feeding TS aggregation. (Proposed Strand-4 "Tower Bench Results Store" decision; Strand 4 is still a future handoff — not yet written.)
votes.lens: right-sized (over- vs under-engineering for tens-to-thousands of bench rows, <100 docs, solo TS/Node vibecoder)
votes.reasoning:
RIGHT-SIZED on every axis the lens cares about, and the load-bearing technical premise checks out against primary sources.

WHY THE CORE CLAIM IS CORRECT (verified, not asserted). Clopper-Pearson bounds ARE Beta quantiles: lo = BetaInv(alpha/2; x, n-x+1), hi = BetaInv(1-alpha/2; x+1, n-x) — the inverse regularized incomplete beta. SQLite's built-in math functions (only present at all with -DSQLITE_ENABLE_MATH_FUNCTIONS) stop at trig/log/pow/sqrt; there is no inverse-beta (sqlite.org/lang_mathfunc.html), and Postgres lacks it natively too. So "CI math cannot live in stock SQL" is literally true, and lifting it to TS pure functions is the only clean option — not a preference. Pure functions are also trivially Vitest-coverable, which matches the design's stated "aggregator pure, Vitest-covered" discipline.

WHY "ZERO BEARING ON ENGINE" HOLDS. Because the only thing SQL does is filter + SUM integer pass/n counts (exact in any engine) and the CI is computed in TS double precision, engine choice is decoupled from correctness. This is the textbook right-sized split: set-ops in SQL, numerics in app code.

WHY IT IS RIGHT-SIZED, NOT OVER/UNDER. Not over-engineered: no vector/graph DB, no data platform; Strand 3 fixes the storage as the thin ResultSink.put(record) contract with an explicit graduation ladder "SQLite -> Postgres -> object store" (SQLite is exactly correct for tens-to-thousands of rows + <100 docs + solo builder). Not under-provisioned: SQLite is ACID/durable single-file, the RunRecord stream is append-only, and a committed results.md scoreboard backs the gitignored runs. A named graduation trigger exists (the ResultSink seam + the SQLite->Postgres ladder), which is precisely what the lens asks for.

HONEST RESIDUALS (caveats, not refutations):
1) LOAD-BEARING SUBTLETY: the stored ci_lo/ci_hi REAL columns are per-record CIs for that row's own n_reps. The leaderboard GROUP BY must NOT average stored CIs (statistically wrong) — it must SUM the (passes, n) counts in SQL and RE-RUN Clopper-Pearson in TS on the folded totals. The claim's phrasing ("GROUP BY feeding TS aggregation") is consistent with this, and it's the exact reason "zero bearing on engine" stays true (integer SUM is engine-exact). But the discipline is conditional: if numeric aggregation ever leaks into SQL (AVG, computing rates), float semantics re-enter and the "zero bearing" guarantee weakens.
2) MILD DENORMALIZATION: materializing ci_lo/ci_hi is derivable from (passes, n). Defensible as a self-describing "CI-carrying RunRecord" audit row + cheap single-record display, but strictly redundant since every leaderboard consumer recomputes in TS anyway. Harmless (two REALs), not over-engineering — just not load-bearing.
3) VALIDATION DEBT: the methodology spec names scipy.stats.binom / R binom as the CI reference. A TS reimplementation must be golden-tested against those, and must handle the x=0 / x=n one-sided edge cases. Reuse a vetted beta-quantile (jStat betainv, @stdlib betaincinv) rather than hand-rolling the inverse incomplete beta — hand-rolled beta quantiles are where numerical bugs hide.

None of these flip the verdict; they are implementation guardrails. The architecture decision itself is correctly sized.

(Tower Bench Results Store — Strand 4 storage architecture for RunRecord data.)
votes.lens: durability — survives without data loss, versioned/reproducible, backed up, artifacts on the filesystem (not DB blobs), index does not silently drift from the docs
votes.reasoning:
The narrow decision survives the durability lens, and on two load-bearing points the evidence is concrete:

1. Lossless round-trip (verified at primary source). SQLite REAL is IEEE-754 binary64 (8-byte double) per sqlite.org/datatype3.html — bit-identical to a JS `number`. Postgres `double precision` is the same. So a TS-computed CP bound stored as a REAL column suffers no precision drift across the named migration path (SQLite to Postgres to object store). "DB engine has zero bearing on statistical correctness" holds: the math never executes in SQL, and the storage medium reproduces the double exactly.

2. Recomputable from raw, not derived-only. The RunRecord schema (strand3-design-B.md:241-249) stores `perLevel: LevelOutcome[] // LPR + raw runs`. Because the raw run counts are persisted, ci_lo/ci_hi are not the sole source of truth — CP is deterministic given (n, k, alpha), so the bounds can always be regenerated. Storing derived REALs is therefore a cache, not a loss vector.

Surrounding durability is also concretely handled: RunRecord is append-only/immutable (one row per agent×tower×N_rep batch — no destructive updates), every row pins agentVersion/towerVersion/taskSetHash/graderVersions/envFingerprint/ipClass for reproducibility, "the log is truth, the leaderboard is a projection" keeps the index derived-from-source rather than a parallel truth, and run artifacts already live on the filesystem (tower/runs/*.png, gitignored) — not as DB blobs — exactly matching the lens's artifact requirement. The pure-function placement makes the math git-versioned and Vitest-coverable.

Genuine durability gaps to nail down in Strand 4 (caveats, not refutations — the claim is narrowly about CI-math placement and DB-independence, and the store itself is explicitly still deferred):
- Backup / source-of-truth medium is unspecified. The design names "SQLite RunRecord store" as the store; a lone .db file as truth is a corruption/loss vector for a solo builder with no backup story. The append-only SHAPE is asserted but the durable MEDIUM is not. The under-engineered, correct fix: write the append-only stream as newline-delimited JSON on the filesystem (committable) and treat SQLite as a rebuildable read index — invert fragility so a corrupt DB is regenerated from the text log.
- The CI method/alpha is not pinned. Pins cover grader/tower versions but not ciMethod=Clopper-Pearson / alpha=0.05 / stat-lib version. Recomputing "durably" from raw runs needs these; different CP implementations (R binom vs scipy vs hand-rolled TS beta-inverse) can disagree at the last ULP near k=0/k=n. Add a statVersion pin.
- Index-vs-docs drift risk is live: tower/results.md is currently a hand-maintained committed scoreboard. Once the RunRecord store exists, results.md must be GENERATED from the log, not hand-edited, or it becomes a second source of truth that drifts — the exact failure the lens names.
- Keep integer (k, n) in the store, not only a REAL pass_rate, so CP inputs stay exact (recovering k from round(pass_rate·n) is a derived-from-derived smell). The "raw runs" field already implies this; the implementation must honor it.

Net: the stated decision is durability-sound and the two facts it stands on (lossless REAL, recomputable-from-raw) check out. The remaining durability work is in the not-yet-built store layer (backup medium, stat-method pin, generated scoreboard), which the claim does not itself assert away.

votes.lens: prior-art (standard tool/pattern to reuse vs reinvention vs cargo-cult)
votes.reasoning:
The architectural decision is the appropriate standard for this scale, not reinvention and not cargo-culting. Two layers:

(1) PLACEMENT (the actual claim) is correct prior-art. Clopper-Pearson requires the inverse incomplete-beta (beta quantile) function, which SQLite core SQL does not provide; doing the CI in SQL would itself be the anti-pattern. The standard pattern for tens-to-thousands of rows is exactly what the design proposes: compute stats in app code, persist ci_lo/ci_hi as columns, and let the store stay a dumb append-only record with a GROUP BY + in-process fold. This makes DB-engine choice genuinely orthogonal to statistical correctness — a sound, well-trodden separation. SQLite is the right-weight store here, not a heavy tool dragged in unnecessarily.

(2) The existence of a maintained library REINFORCES rather than refutes the claim: @stdlib/stats-binomial-test ships the exact (Clopper-Pearson) interval as a pure JS/TS function. I verified the source — lower = betaQuantile(alpha/2, x, n-x+1), upper = betaQuantile(1-alpha/2, x+1, n-x), which is textbook Clopper-Pearson via inverse incomplete beta. That a battle-tested package implements this as a pure function is direct evidence that 'CI math lives in TS, not SQL' is the standard path.

The single caveat sits BELOW the claim's altitude: the phrase 'pure functions' is ambiguous about hand-rolling vs wrapping. Hand-rolling the regularized-incomplete-beta inverse is reinventing a numerically fiddly solved problem — it should wrap @stdlib/stats-binomial-test (or jStat beta.inv as a thinner dep). With that reuse, the claim is fully sound; the decision is neither over- nor under-engineered. Note this lens is scoped to build-vs-reuse; the separate methodology question (Clopper-Pearson's known conservatism vs Wilson) is out of scope and already acknowledged in the repo's own scoring doc, which lists 'Wilson/Clopper-Pearson CIs'.

votes.claim: The Tower Bench Results Store should split durability by data type: SQLite .db binary (gitignored, backed up via the SQLite .backup API) + a JSONL export committed to git in tower/results/ as the human-readable, diff-friendly audit trail — "this dual-format pattern is how serious research bench projects (Metriq, AgentLab result dirs) handle append-only scored data."
votes.lens: right-sized (tens-to-thousands of result rows, <100 curated docs, solo TS/Node vibecoder who hates over-engineering; skeptic about both over- and under-engineering)
votes.reasoning:
Refuted on two grounds: a false precedent and mild over-provisioning for the actual scale.

(1) The justifying authority is factually wrong. The claim leans on Metriq and AgentLab as exemplars of the SQLite-plus-git-JSONL dual format. Primary sources contradict this. AgentLab's README stores results as a home-directory tree (AGENTLAB_EXP_ROOT, default ~/agentlab-results) of per-experiment folders loaded into a pandas dataframe via ExpResult/load_result_df — neither SQLite nor git-committed JSONL, and the home-dir default means they aren't committed to git at all (they're local run artifacts; internally json summaries plus pickled args/steps). Metriq (arXiv 2603.08680) is explicitly "a modular, file-based design that... avoids reliance on centralized databases," exchanging results "exclusively through version-controlled artifacts." So Metriq endorses the files-in-git half but argues AGAINST the database half, and AgentLab uses neither piece of the cited pattern. Both named exemplars point AWAY from a backed-up SQLite binary, not toward it. The lens demands primary-source grounding; the primary sources debunk the citation.

(2) For the real scale the dual format with a .backup ritual is over-built. The design itself specifies a SEQUENTIAL runner (single writer) and tens-to-thousands of append-only rows (N_rep>=10 per cell). At that scale a git-committed JSONL/NDJSON file IS already the complete durability story: git history gives durability, CI, audit trail, diff, and reproducibility for free, and thousands of rows parse into Node memory in well under 100ms, covering the "leaderboard fold = pure read filtered by towerVersion." The SQLite .backup API specifically solves hot-copy-under-concurrency — a problem a single-writer solo bench does not have. Maintaining TWO co-equal durable representations plus a concurrency-grade backup ceremony duplicates durability that git already provides.

This is NOT egregious over-engineering — SQLite+files+git is exactly the lens's named-acceptable tier, not a vector/graph DB, and the surrounding design even names a graduation path (SQLite -> Postgres -> object store). But the claim as stated over-specifies: the right-sized shape is JSONL-in-git as the single source of truth (durability + CI + audit), with SQLite demoted to an OPTIONAL, gitignored, REBUILDABLE query cache/index regenerated from the JSONL — therefore needing no separate .backup at all. The claim instead frames a backed-up SQLite binary and a parallel committed JSONL as co-equal necessities justified by a misattributed precedent. That framing is both factually unsupported and slightly heavier than the data warrants, so it fails the right-sized test.

votes.claim: The Tower results store should use a gitignored SQLite .db as the primary store (backed up via the SQLite .backup API) plus a JSONL export committed to git in tower/results/ as the human-readable, diff-friendly, reproducible audit trail - a dual-format pattern attributed to Metriq and AgentLab result dirs.
votes.reasoning:
Refuted on durability for two independent reasons; the JSONL-in-git half is correct and worth keeping.

(1) Inverted source of truth = drift and loss hazard. Making the gitignored .db the PRIMARY write target and the committed JSONL a DERIVED export is exactly the silent-drift pattern this lens rejects. Git reflects reality only when someone remembers to export and commit, so the committed audit trail lags the live .db between runs. The .db is durable only via a manual, out-of-band .backup of a gitignored, unversioned, non-diffable file; rows written but not yet exported are lost if the .db is lost. For tens-to-thousands of rows this is two stores that can disagree = both over-engineered AND a correctness hazard. The SQLite .backup API claim is technically true (it does take a consistent hot snapshot) but only solves a problem you create by choosing a single-binary DB as primary; an append-only JSONL in git makes every commit a consistent, versioned, diffable snapshot for free, so the .backup machinery is accidental complexity.

(2) The appeal-to-precedent is false (verified against primary sources). The Metriq paper (arxiv 2603.08680) explicitly states its architecture avoids reliance on centralized databases and exchanges results exclusively through version-controlled artifacts; metriq-data is a GitHub repo of version-controlled JSON aggregated into dist/, with NO SQLite. AgentLab stores a directory of per-experiment files (pickle + json) under AGENTLAB_EXP_ROOT (~/agentlab-results), lazy-loaded via ExpResult, with NO SQLite/.db, and those dirs are local, not committed to git. Neither cited project uses the SQLite-primary + JSONL-export dual format attributed to them. The real precedent points the opposite way: a single file-based source of truth, no database in the durability path.

(3) Internal evidence agrees. The repo's own research (tower/research/2026-06-27-02-scoring-methodology.md:256, 2026-06-27-03-tower-design.md:181, strand3-design-B.md:252, strand3-design-C.md:229) already frames the store as a flat append-only RunRecord log behind a ResultSink.put() seam with the leaderboard as a pure fold; tower/results.md is a committed flat scoreboard and PNG artifacts already live in gitignored tower/runs/.

The version that survives (and is LESS code): JSONL append-only committed to git = the SINGLE source of truth (versioning + backup + reproducibility + diffability for free). SQLite, if wanted at all, is a throwaway DERIVED query index rebuilt from the JSONL, gitignored, needing zero backup. Artifacts (PNG/pcap) stay as path-referenced files under gitignored tower/runs/, never blobs in a DB. votes.lens: prior-art: is there a standard pattern to reuse, or is this reinventing / cargo-culting?
votes.reasoning:
The load-bearing justification — that Metriq and AgentLab use this dual-format SQLite+JSONL pattern — is factually wrong, and the actual prior art points to a SIMPLER single-format standard that makes the SQLite layer unnecessary at this scale.

What the cited projects actually do:
- Metriq (metriq-data / metriq-gym, Unitary Foundation): stores results as schema-validated JSON files in a directory/file-system layout committed directly to a git repo. Their own docs: the dataset "can be reproduced, versioned, and analyzed just by cloning the repository." There is NO SQLite binary and NO separate binary-vs-export split. The committed structured text IS the single source of truth. (The metriq.info web platform is a separate web app; it is not the bench results store being modeled here.)
- AgentLab (ServiceNow): writes per-experiment result directories (pickle blobs + a summary_info.json) under AGENTLAB_EXP_ROOT (default ~/agentlab_results), lazily loaded via ExpResult and aggregated into a pandas DataFrame by load_result_df. These live in a user home dir, are NOT committed to git, and use NO SQLite. Single format, transient, query-via-pandas.

So neither exemplar uses "gitignored SQLite + committed JSONL export." Both use a SINGLE format. The proposed design is therefore not reusing their pattern — it adds a layer (a second source of truth + an export/sync step + .backup plumbing) that neither named project has.

On the engineering merits at the stated scale (tens-to-thousands of append-only scored rows, solo TS/Node builder): the genuine standard for "human-readable, diff-friendly, reproducible, committed audit trail" is exactly ONE committed text artifact — JSONL or directory-of-JSON. That is what Metriq does, and what the wider eval-harness ecosystem does (lm-evaluation-harness emits JSON/JSONL; inspect_ai uses per-run log files; OpenAI evals use JSONL). For append-only data at this size you do not need indexed/concurrent query support, so SQLite earns little, and maintaining BOTH a binary .db AND a derived JSONL in sync is a classic correctness-burden over-engineering (two sources of truth that can drift; .backup snapshots add ops with no payoff). Note SQLite itself is not "heavy" — it is the canonical lightweight embedded DB and would be a fine SINGLE choice; the problem is specifically the dual-write/sync architecture justified by a fabricated prior-art precedent.

Recommendation implied by the prior art: pick one. Either commit JSONL (or schema-validated per-row JSON, Metriq-style) as the single store/audit trail, or use SQLite alone and generate JSONL only on demand for diffs — but do not run two persisted sources of truth with .backup plumbing at this scale. The "dual-format is how serious benches do it" premise is not supported by the projects named.

Both load-bearing choices match the real scale, and the design explicitly rejects the over-engineered alternatives.

1) SQLite as the truth store is right-sized, not over- and not under-provisioned. The RunRecord workload is read-heavy, append-only, single-writer (solo builder, build-time regen) — SQLite's exact sweet spot; primary sources confirm it outperforms server DBs for read-heavy small datasets and that its only real disqualifier (high-concurrency multi-user) does not apply to a published scoreboard. It is NOT over-engineered: the survey scope (Strand-4 reframe spec, docs/specs/2026-06-27-bench-reframe-and-research-loop-design.md §4) lists vector/graph/columnar/document options, and choosing plain relational SQLite over DuckDB/graph/vector is correct at thousands of rows — the aggregation work (Clopper–Pearson CIs, group-by tool×detector×time, overlapping-CI 'tie' comparator) is genuinely relational, which is precisely what justifies SQLite over a pile of JSON files rather than something heavier. It is NOT under-provisioned: SQLite is a real ACID store, and the design correctly keeps artifacts (PNGs/pcaps) on the filesystem referenced by path, never blobs in the DB.

2) Static-site generation over a live-query server is right-sized for a read-only, build-time-updated artifact. A bench scoreboard's freshness window is 'whenever a new run is recorded' (hours/days), not real-time — the case where primary sources say SSG is preferred and a live query server is unwarranted. SSG removes an always-on process/hosting surface (matching the solo low-maintenance budget) while a Fastify-queries-SQLite-per-request server would add ops burden for zero benefit on read-only published results. The 'store is truth, site is a regenerable snapshot' framing is the correct durability separation: durability lives at the store layer (the SQLite file must be committed/backed up — the §4 spec already calls for 'backups for results'), and the site can be thrown away and rebuilt.

The Strand-3 handoff (tower/research/2026-06-27-03-tower-design.md, 'Handoff to Strands 4 & 5') names the explicit migration path SQLite → Postgres → object store and fixes the leaderboard as 'a pure read over RunRecords ... at render time' — matching the claim verbatim. The reframe spec §6 adds concrete grep→richer-store triggers (terminology drift, unstructured volume, ~50-doc threshold).

Residuals (honest, not disqualifying): (a) the claim-as-stated names no graduation trigger itself — it relies on the surrounding design supplying one; the SSG-specific trigger (when you'd need per-user auth/RLS, real-time freshness, or interactive ad-hoc queries → a server) is implied but never spelled out for the scoreboard. (b) Binary SQLite in git diffs/merges poorly; fine for a solo append-only writer, or dump to .sql text for git-friendliness — an implementation detail, not an architecture flaw. (c) Durability is only as good as actually backing up the single SQLite file, since the site layer is explicitly disposable. None of these flip the verdict; the architecture matches the data scale with a named graduation path.

votes.reasoning:
The claim has two halves, and they don't share a verdict.

HALF 1 — "store is truth, site is a read-only build-time projection, static-gen not a live server." Durability-SOUND, keep it. A regenerable, disposable published site can never itself be a source of loss, and drift between site and truth self-heals on every rebuild — exactly the no-drift property the lens demands. The design docs already endorse this verbatim: "the log is the truth, the view is a projection" (scoring-methodology.md:266) and "the leaderboard renderer is a pure read over RunRecords" (strand3-design-B.md:252). For tens-to-thousands of rows there is no live-query need; static-gen is correct.

HALF 2 — "the SQLite RunRecord store is the truth." As stated this is NOT concretely durable, and it risks loss + irreproducibility, which the lens scores as refuted:

1) Single-point-of-loss / no backup. A single SQLite binary would BE the entire append-only audit record, yet the repo's established pattern is that tower run outputs are gitignored — confirmed: `tower/runs/` is in .gitignore:47 and `git check-ignore` returns the PNGs (exit 0). Drop the DB there (the natural place) and the truth store is un-versioned, un-backed-up by the git remote, and one disk failure from total loss. The claim states no backup story at all.

2) Regresses git-auditability. This is a public, build-in-the-open, reproducibility-valuing solo project whose CURRENT truth is a committed markdown table (`tower/results.md`) — diffable, reviewable, restorable from any clone. An opaque SQLite binary cannot be meaningfully diffed, reviewed, or merge-resolved in git, so it discards the free, durable, human-auditable version history the project already relies on.

3) The data-volume argument is inverted. The claim invokes "this data volume" to justify SQLite, but tens-to-thousands of small JSON records is precisely the scale where committed append-only JSONL / per-run JSON files are STRICTLY more durable: versioned + diffable + backed up by every clone + human-auditable, at zero maintenance cost. SQLite's real advantages (indexed query at large volume, concurrent writes) don't bite here; its durability costs do. Tellingly, the design docs nominate JSON as the canonical serialization ("a flat append-only log of run records," Online-Mind2Web result.json schema — scoring-methodology.md:256-266), and call storage "storage-agnostic ... SQLite → Postgres → object store ... the orchestrator does not care if that's SQLite, Postgres, or flat files" (strand3-design-C.md:229), explicitly DEFERRING the tech to Strand 4. The claim hardens a deliberately-deferred, storage-agnostic decision into the least git-durable of the flat options.

4) Artifact-blob risk left unpinned. Artifacts are already large (3.7MB PNGs today; future pcaps/HAR/trajectory tapes) and the design correctly keeps them as filesystem "artifact pointers." But "SQLite is truth" creates pressure to inline blobs, and the claim doesn't pin the filesystem-artifacts-with-DB-pointers rule — leaving the lens's "artifacts safe on the filesystem, not blobs in a DB" requirement unhandled.

Net: the projection/static-gen SHAPE is right and reproducibility pins (task_set_hash, tower_version, grader_versions, env fingerprint — scoring-methodology.md:251) are durability-positive, but the specific "SQLite is the truth store" choice, as stated, risks total loss (un-backed-up single binary, matching the gitignored-runs pattern) and irreproducibility (no git audit trail). Cheap fix that flips every box green: make truth = committed append-only JSONL / per-run JSON in git (the design's own canonical schema), and treat any SQLite/derived index as a disposable build-time projection generated alongside the site — same as the scoreboard itself. That keeps the correct "truth-store + reproducible read-only projection" spine while restoring versioning, backup, auditability, and filesystem-safe artifacts.

votes.lens: prior-art (reuse-vs-reinvent / over-vs-under-engineering)
votes.reasoning:
The decision matches the canonical standard for this data shape, and it correctly rejects the heavier option rather than cargo-culting it.

WHAT THE DATA ACTUALLY IS (from tower/research/2026-06-27-03-tower-design.md and strand3-design-B.md): the RunRecord stream is append-only, immutable, version-stamped (one row per agent×tower×N_rep batch). It changes ONLY when a bench run executes — never per-user, never real-time. The leaderboard is already specified as "a pure read over RunRecords... applied at render time" and "a projection; the log is the truth." That is textbook event-log + read-model (CQRS) thinking, and rendering a read-model at build time onto static files is exactly the Jamstack/static-projection pattern (Observable's SSG definition: run the queries/transform once at build, ship the result as files). So the architectural CATEGORY chosen is the established standard, not an invention.

WHY THE REJECTED OPTION IS THE OVER-ENGINEERED ONE: a live-query server (Postgres + API + always-on host) buys real-time freshness and concurrent-write query performance — neither of which exists here (data is tiny, immutable, and refreshed only on a manual bench run). For a solo TS/Node maintainer who hates over-engineering, standing up and operating a query server for hundreds-to-low-thousands of static rows is the cargo-cult choice. The claim argues AGAINST that, which is the correct skeptical call.

WHERE IT NEEDS A GUARDRAIL (honest caveat, not a refutation): "static-site generation" must NOT be read as "adopt a full SSG framework (Astro/Eleventy/Hugo)." At <100 curated docs plus a few tables, the lightest valid member of that family is a ~50-line Node build script that reads SQLite and emits HTML/Markdown — which the repo ALREADY does today via the committed tower/results.md. Pulling in a framework + its plugin ecosystem would itself be mild over-engineering for this volume. The claim's wording leaves room for the light version (good), but the team should consciously default to the build-script end of the spectrum, not the framework end.

NAMED PRIOR ART THEY SHOULD CONSCIOUSLY REJECT (so the choice is informed, not accidental): Datasette / Datasette Lite (Simon Willison) is THE maintained tool for "read-only SQLite → publishable, even fully-static-WASM, explorable site." It is the closest off-the-shelf substitute. It is a justified NON-FIT here, not a missed reuse, for two concrete reasons: (1) it is Python, off the project's deliberate TS/Node-native spine; and (2) the scoreboard carries domain logic at render time — the overlapping-Clopper–Pearson-CI → "tie" comparator, version/taskSetHash filtering, and the cap/det/sec radar — which a generic SQLite-publish explorer cannot express, so they'd still hand-write the projection. Documenting this rejection is the only gap; the decision itself survives it.

NET: confirmed — build-time static projection over an authoritative store is the appropriate standard for append-only, build-triggered, low-volume data under a solo maintenance budget, and rejecting a live-query server is the correct anti-over-engineering call. Tighten only by (a) defaulting to a plain build script over a heavy SSG framework at this scale, and (b) recording Datasette as a considered-and-rejected reuse.

votes.lens: prior-art (standard tool reuse vs reinventing / cargo-culting)
votes.claim: Observable Plot covers time-series natively and handles the radar via the azimuthal-equidistant projection workaround; if that workaround's fragility is unacceptable for CI bands on the radar, Apache ECharts 6.0 can replace the radar component only — its radar series natively supports area bands for CIs and bundles to a ~200 KB static chunk.
votes.reasoning:
Half the claim is fine, but the escape hatch — the part actually being stress-tested — rests on a false premise and an unnecessary heavy dependency.

WHAT HOLDS: Observable Plot is the correct, maintained standard for the time-series view at this scale (tens-to-thousands of rows). And CI bands on the TIME-SERIES are native in Plot via band/area marks (areaY with y1/y2), so Plot needs no help there. That portion is confirmed-appropriate.

WHAT FAILS:
(1) FALSE FACTUAL PREMISE. The justification for pulling in ECharts is "its radar series natively supports area bands for CIs." It does not. ECharts radar areaStyle fills the polygon from the center axis outward to the data line (origin:auto) — a solid fill, not a band between an upper and lower bound. Producing a real CI band on a radar requires overlaying two polygons and faking the in-between fill, the same stacked-series hack ECharts users apply to line-chart confidence bands (apache/echarts#12592, widely described as "a hack"). So swapping to ECharts does NOT buy native CI bands — you trade one hack for an equivalent hack plus a second charting engine. The premise that motivates the whole fallback is wrong.

(2) UNNECESSARY HEAVY SECOND DEPENDENCY. Running two charting libraries (Plot + ECharts) on a scoreboard of <few-thousand rows, for one solo TS/Node builder who hates over-engineering, is the cargo-cult smell — and it's bought on the false premise above. ECharts is ~1 MB full / ~200 KB tree-shaken; that's a real per-page cost for one radar.

(3) THE STANDARD ANSWER IS SIMPLER AND THE RADAR IS THE WRONG CHART ANYWAY. Observable themselves publish "Why you should avoid radar charts" (axis-order distortion, meaningless connecting lines, no room for labels, poor comparison). Their recommended replacements — grouped bars, small multiples, parallel coordinates, or a plain table — are ALL native Plot marks with no projection hack and trivial native CI bands. The genuinely reuse-the-standard move is: keep Plot for everything and drop the radar for small-multiples/parallel-coordinates, OR (if a single engine is preferred for both views) standardize on ECharts alone (native time-series + radar, dark mode, one dep) — but even then radar CI bands stay a manual overlay, which is itself an argument against the radar. Either single-library path beats a two-library setup justified by a capability that doesn't exist.

NET: the decision reinvents fragility (the projection radar) and then cargo-cults a heavy second tool to "fix" it on a mistaken native-CI-band claim, at a scale where one library plus a better-suited mark is the maintained, lighter standard.

votes.claim: The curated corpus has exceeded the nominal 50-doc threshold but is well-partitioned into named directories; the threshold flags when grep becomes a probabilistic hunt, which has not happened yet for single-concept searches within a known path — so no graduation to a richer store is warranted.
votes.lens: right-sized
votes.reasoning:
The decision is to STAY on grep + structured directories + git rather than graduate to a vector/graph/search-platform store. For a solo TS/Node builder with a few-hundred hand-written docs, that is the textbook right-sized choice — adopting a vector DB or graph DB here would be clear over-engineering, and the refusal avoids it. It is also not under-provisioned: git supplies versioning/durability for all text, and the governing spec (docs/specs/2026-06-27-bench-reframe-and-research-loop-design.md §4) already mandates polyglot persistence, filesystem artifacts referenced by path (never blobs in DB), and backups for results.

Crucially, the lens's bar — "matches the real scale WITH a named graduation trigger" — is met emphatically. The same spec's §6 enumerates not one but FIVE concrete, monitored triggers: terminology drift, unstructured volume (querying raw transcripts/run-logs), context overflow, the 3-grep rule, and the rough ~50-curated-doc line. The claim's framing that the 50 number is a *flag* (not a hard cutoff) faithfully matches the spec, which says "past that, OR once querying raw transcripts → richer store." That is exactly the disciplined "named graduation trigger" that distinguishes right-sizing from optimism.

Two honest caveats that I weighed but that do not flip the verdict: (1) The claim's literal figures are understated/over-simplified — the repo actually has 468 git-tracked md/txt files (~514K words), not 185/310K, and it collapses the spec's five-condition trigger into a single soft number. (2) Partitioning is real at the top level but some leaf directories are dense (docs/specs = 74 files; journal/ops/sessions and journal/ops/archive = 70 each), and the 100+ date-named session/raw-archive artifacts ARE the 'unstructured volume' the spec names as a trigger. But these artifacts are date-addressed handoffs nobody queries by content, and the claim explicitly scopes itself to 'single-concept searches within a known path,' which remains true because files are date+topic-named. Within that scope, grep has not degraded into a probabilistic hunt, and the early-warning triggers are armed to fire before it does. That is right-sized.

votes.lens: durability — does the corpus survive: no data loss, versioned/reproducible, backed up, artifacts as files on disk (not DB blobs), and no index silently drifting from the docs.
votes.reasoning: Through the durability lens the underlying decision (keep the corpus as plain, directory-partitioned markdown in one git monorepo) is concretely durable. (1) Versioned + offsite-backed: 458 tracked .md files in a single repo pushed to GitHub origin — appropriate, not over- or under-engineered for a solo builder with <500 docs. (2) Files on the filesystem, not DB blobs: no sqlite/DB exists; the corpus is directories of .md. (3) The only structured store, graphify-out/*.json, is gitignored AND deterministically regenerable by the post-commit hook (~2s, no LLM) — a derived cache, not a precious artifact. (4) That derived index cannot drift the corpus: /.graphifyignore explicitly fences ALL markdown, docs/, journal/, research/, blog/, skills/ out of the code graph, so the one automated index indexes code only and structurally cannot go stale against the doc corpus. (5) The human-facing index, journal/docs-map.md, is a coarse role-map (which doc owns what), not a per-file enumeration, so it can't silently drift per file; the phase-end 'reconcile to reality / leave the docs true' ritual is the correction path, and session handoffs are append-only. The partitioning itself is just real git-tracked directories — fully versioned, zero loss risk. Honest residual (operational, not architectural): right now dev is 1 commit ahead of origin, 6 tracked files are dirty, and 8 untracked non-ignored .md exist — including 7 fresh curated corpus docs under tower/research/ that live only on local disk until committed+pushed. That is the standard mid-session unpushed window, closable with one commit+push, not a structural irreproducibility/drift flaw. The 286 untracked-ignored .md (superpowers/council/inbox/local) are intentionally transient and correctly excluded. Net: durability is concretely handled; the claim survives the lens, with a hygiene note to push the new tower/research docs.

votes.claim: The curated corpus (~185 files / 310K words, actually ~226 files / 325K words for docs+research+blog) has passed the nominal 50-doc threshold, but staying on grep over named directories is fine because the threshold's real trigger — grep becoming a probabilistic hunt — hasn't hit for single-concept searches within a known path.
votes.lens: prior-art (reuse-a-standard vs reinvent vs cargo-cult-a-heavy-tool)
votes.reasoning:
From the prior-art lens the only question that matters is: at this scale, is grep-over-partitioned-dirs the appropriate maintained standard, or are they (a) reinventing a solved search problem or (b) cargo-culting a heavy tool? It's neither — it's the right standard, and the heavy alternatives would be the actual over-engineering.

1) grep/ripgrep IS the standard tool here, by primary-source guidance. ripgrep's maintainer (BurntSushi) states indexing is only worth it when the corpus does not fit in memory; "if your corpus fits into memory, then ripgrep's existing search is probably fast enough." 325K words is ~2-3MB of text (even the full 569K-word md tree is ~4MB) — it fits in memory hundreds of times over. So there is no maintained index/search tool to "reuse instead": the standard tool for this scale already is grep. Adopting Elasticsearch/Lunr/Tantivy/a vector DB/a RAG pipeline at <3MB would be cargo-culting a heavy tool unnecessarily — exactly the failure the lens warns against.

2) They are not reinventing anything either. The corpus is backed by the two standard companion patterns to grep, both already present: an index/manifest (journal/docs-map.md — an explicit "source of truth" map, the docs-index pattern; cf. llms.txt-style manifests) and a semantic-Q&A layer (docs/feather_notebooklm_pack/ → NotebookLM) aimed at precisely the fuzzy/cross-cutting "where did we decide X" queries that grep handles badly. So the one genuine weak spot of grep (recall on concept search, not speed) is already covered by an off-the-shelf tool rather than a hand-rolled one. The stack is directory partitioning + manifest index + ripgrep + NotebookLM — all standard, all reused, zero custom search infrastructure.

3) The claim's own framing is the correct engineering instinct: it treats the 50-doc number as a *nominal* heuristic and re-checks it against the real failure mode (probabilistic hunt) instead of mechanically acting on the count. (The 50 itself is a self-invented internal heuristic, not an industry standard, but it's used as a flag, not cargo-culted as a hard rule — which is fine.)

Skeptic check both directions: under-engineering? No — grep is the maintainer-endorsed standard for an in-memory corpus, and the semantic gap is plugged by NotebookLM. Over-engineering? Also avoided — they declined to bolt on a search index/DB that this scale doesn't justify. The only caveat is bookkeeping: the curated count is ~226 files/325K words (and 495/569K including journal+archives), modestly larger than the claim's 185/310K, but still squarely in grep's comfort zone, so the verdict is unchanged. The threshold to actually revisit this is not file count but the day single-concept grep starts returning too many cross-directory hits to triage by hand — and even then the standard next step is ripgrep's own optional indexing or leaning harder on NotebookLM, not a bespoke system.
